summary: We built Earth Symphony, a multisensory "Earth Jukebox" that turns NASA climate maps into music, speech and touch, so anyone, including people who are blind or have low vision, can explore planetary data without seeing the map. It runs in any browser, with no installation, in English and Portuguese. Four global NASA GEOS maps (air temperature, humidity, near-surface wind and carbon monoxide pollution) become an orchestra: each variable has its own instrument (piano, flute, harp and marimba), higher values play higher notes, and the map's left and right sides play in the left and right ears. Ambient sounds tell users where they are without words: waves over the ocean, icy wind at the poles, birds over forests. Press Space and a voice says "Brazil. Temperature 27.3 degrees Celsius." Scan a QR code and your phone vibrates with the value under the cursor. Everything works with one-key keyboard shortcuts and screen readers, and color-blind-safe palettes fix rainbow scales. Climate data is published almost only as colored maps, yet 2.2 billion people live with vision impairment (WHO). Earth Symphony makes NASA data something you can hear and feel.
details:
Close your eyes. Now read a weather map.

Climate science speaks almost only in color. Temperature anomalies, pollution plumes and storm tracks reach the public as colored maps, often with rainbow scales. For the 43 million people who are blind and 295 million with moderate to severe vision impairment worldwide (IAPB Vision Atlas, 2020), and for roughly 1 in 12 men with color-vision deficiency, these maps are closed doors. In Brazil alone, 7.9 million people have permanent difficulty seeing (IBGE Census 2022). People with disabilities are also hit hardest by climate disasters: the UN reports they can die at two to four times the rate of the general population (UNDRR, 2023). Earth Symphony opens that door: it lets anyone hear, hear spoken and feel NASA's view of the planet.

What it does

Earth Symphony is a browser-based "Earth Jukebox" that turns four global NASA GMAO GEOS maps into an explorable, multisensory experience:

Each map is a sequence of 372 hourly frames, from 30 October 2026 09:00 UTC to 14 November 2026 20:00 UTC. Users can step hour by hour or press play and hear the planet change with the cursor standing still.

How it works

  1. Reading NASA's maps back into numbers. The app reads the map images NASA GMAO publishes, not raw files. A Python tool samples each official color bar column by column and generates the lookup tables. In the browser, every pixel is converted to the perceptually uniform CIELAB color space, matched to the nearest color on the bar and projected onto the neighboring segment to get a continuous value. Reading uses the median of a 5×5 window, which removes coastlines, borders and JPEG noise; the GMAO logo and timestamp are masked. The carbon monoxide bar is non-linear, so its tick marks were measured pixel by pixel; the wind map's transparent "calm" band has its own rule.
  2. Validated against NASA's own colors. Over 12,000 pixels per variable, the median color error is ΔE 1.0 to 2.3, around the just-noticeable difference for human vision (ΔE ≈ 2.3). Sanity checks match known geography: the equatorial Pacific reads 28.8 °C, Antarctica −39.7 °C, Amazon humidity 19 g/kg and eastern China CO 311 ppbv.
  3. Data to sound (sonification), built with Tone.js. One instrument per variable. Higher values play higher notes, quantized to a major pentatonic scale (C or G) with hysteresis so notes do not flicker at boundaries. The cursor's horizontal position becomes stereo position: the left of the map plays in the left ear, the right in the right ear.
  4. Sounds of places. Under the instrument, ambient sound tells users where they are without words: ocean waves, icy wind and crystals over ice, insects and birds over forests, dry wind over deserts. A land/ocean mask generated from the wind frames decides the landscape.
  5. A voice on demand. Clicking or pressing Space speaks the country and value ("Brazil. Temperature 27.3 degrees Celsius"), using Natural Earth country borders. Music pauses while the voice speaks and comes back on its own, so two sounds never compete. Only one narration plays at a time.
  6. Navigation without sight. Every action has a single-key shortcut, with no Ctrl/Alt/Shift: arrows move the cursor (hold to go faster); keys 1–9 jump to nine map regions like a phone keypad; Space reads the value; O gives an overview (highest, lowest, where they are, and the average); C gives position and coordinates; V starts a sound tour where the cursor wanders the map; P, [ and ] control the timeline; H opens help; T opens the tutorial; I switches English/Portuguese. The color bar is playable too. The map is an ARIA application with live regions, managed focus and labelled controls for NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver and TalkBack.
  7. Touch. A QR code pairs the phone with the computer. PeerJS only handles signaling; the data then flows peer-to-peer over WebRTC. The phone vibrates with the value under the cursor: short, fast pulses for high values, long, slow pulses for low ones, with a double pulse when crossing zones. iPhones, which block web vibration, show visual pulses instead. A "copy receiver link" button helps users who cannot see the QR code.
  8. Low vision and color blindness. Larger text (the map cursor grows with it), high contrast that respects prefers-contrast, color-blind-safe palettes that recolor the map from the decoded data (Cividis, Viridis, grayscale), simulations of color-vision deficiencies, and prefers-reduced-motion support.
  9. A five-minute audio tutorial for blind users. It opens on the first visit, works with keyboard and sound only, and is recorded in English and Portuguese. It teaches the shortcuts, plays each instrument from lowest to highest value, demonstrates left/right stereo and the place sounds, then gives hands-on challenges on the real temperature map: move the cursor, find out where you are, find the cold of Antarctica (the lowest piano notes), return to the center, move forward one hour.
